strengths: Explicitly rejects 'Japan invented shared streets' and the all-streets-lack-sidewalks stereotype
Arterials, new towns, and station plazas are named as the counter-pattern
Shopfronts and leftover width versus a named design movement are handled without mystique

issues.location: ## Why the Sidewalk Was Never Built — 20 km/h vs 50 km/h
issues.problem: Humane-at-20 / fragile-at-50 is European shared-space language. Japanese residential practice is not designed around those two numbers; Zone 30 already appears earlier as 30 km/h municipal work.
issues.suggestion: Drop the 20/50 pair. Say slow crawling versus arterial behavior, or stay with Zone 30 already in the piece. Do not invent a Japanese design speed.

issues.location: ## Why the Sidewalk Was Never Built — Setback roads / Article 42-2
issues.problem: Naming Article 42-2 as if it were the general sidewalk story over-legalizes and over-generalizes. Many no-sidewalk streets are already ordinary 4 m-class living roads, not only 2-項 setback lanes.
issues.suggestion: Hedge: lot-by-lot setback widening is one slow process on some older sub-standard lanes; many other neighborhood roads have no curb simply because the existing width fits a car, not two sidewalks. Do not quiz readers on the article number.

issues.problem: 'Few streetlights' is too absolute; lighting varies widely by municipality and era of development.
issues.suggestion: Say lighting varies, or 'a dim grid,' not that residential Japan is generally unlit.
